response.consequence: In credential-sync mode, parsed refresh results lose expiry_date, expires_in and other fields. The stored credentials then look expired or lack expiry information, so tokens are refreshed repeatedly or integrations break. Callers such as the Zoom adapter that read newTokens.expires_in get undefined.
response.explanation: The schema keys are `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Calling toString() on a Zod schema object returns "[object Object]". The schema therefore requires a literal property named "[object Object]" to be a number. The second computed key is the same string, so it overwrites the first and makes that property optional unknown. Real token responses (access_token, expires_in and so on) have no such property. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the second key overwrites the first in the object literal, so the number requirement is probably dropped. The schema is then effectively just access_token plus the default strip behaviour. That strips expires_in and other fields, because z.object strips unknown keys by default. The intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' and 'allow other properties' logic is not implemented. As a result, expiry fields are dropped from the parsed data.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that stringify to "[object Object]", so credential-sync parsing always fails

response.consequence: With credential sync on, callers receive parsed data without expiry fields, and the stored refresh token is replaced with the fake string "refresh_token". Zoom's refresh code (VideoApiAdapter.ts:119-124) writes that string into the credential's refresh_token. It also computes expiry_date as `Date.now() + undefined * 1000`, which is NaN. Later refreshes then send the bogus refresh token to the provider and fail, so the integration breaks.
response.explanation: `z.string().toString()` and `z.string().optional().toString()` are both "[object Object]", so the second computed key overwrites the first. The schema is therefore `{access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown.optional()}`. It has no number-valued expiry rule and no catch-all. Zod's default strip mode removes every other field, including expires_in, expiry_date and refresh_token. The next step in parseRefreshTokenResponse then sees refresh_token as missing and sets it to the literal "refresh_token". This happens whenever credential sync is enabled and the endpoint is configured.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are not wildcards; expiry fields are stripped and refresh_token is replaced by a placeholder

response.consequence: With credential sync on, hubspot credentials are overwritten in the DB with a serialized Response and a NaN expiry, which breaks the integration for that user. Google tokens never refresh and fail silently. Webex and zoom pass the Response to their own response handlers, so they were not shown to break.
response.explanation: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the fetch Response from the sync endpoint. It does not check the status, parse the body, or normalize the result. The non-sync branch returns whatever each caller's refresh function produces: the hubspot SDK token object, or the google `res` with `.data`. Hubspot types the result as HubspotToken and reads `.expiresIn` from it. A Response has no `expiresIn`, so `expiryDate` becomes NaN. The Response is then written to `credential.key` in the DB. Google reads `res?.data`, which is undefined on a Response, so `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The surrounding catch treats any message other than invalid_grant as a no-op, so the refresh silently fails. The sync request also sends no auth header, so the endpoint cannot verify the caller. That last point comes from the code only, and I did not check what the endpoint requires.
response.title: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response in sync mode, which hubspot and google misread as a token object
